q: Does the beta-vs-alpha anti-correlation hold at PIDE scale (~150 cell lines) when the per-line (eps_i, eps_c) fits are re-derived under a modern optimizer, rather than inherited from Herr 2014 Table 2 (17 lines)?
basis: Our 17-line subset gave Pearson r(alpha, beta) = +0.655, opposite sign to the paper's headline claim. Herr 2014 shows eps_i and eps_c themselves strongly co-vary in this subset, masking the predicted anti-correlation. The paper's original claim was anchored on the full ~150-line PIDE dataset.
next_steps: Pull the PIDE v3 database (Friedrich 2013 IJRB companion paper) or re-digitise Friedrich 2012 Fig. 5. Refit (eps_i, eps_c) per line against clonogenic data using an L-BFGS optimizer with sensible priors. Recompute Pearson and Spearman correlations at full scale. Report whether the anti-correlation survives and, if so, over which alpha-range and dose-window it is strongest. All feasible free-endpoint on a laptop.

q: How sensitive is the GLDM survival curve to replacing the paper's uniform-Poisson placement of DSBs into N_L identical loops with a realistic Hi-C-informed loop-length distribution (fat-tailed, cell-type-specific)?
basis: The paper fixes N_L = 3000 identical loops. Modern Hi-C data (e.g., 4DN, ENCODE) resolves loop domains at kbp-to-Mbp scale with a heavy-tailed length distribution that varies between differentiated cell types. The clustered-DSB probability p_c is nonlinear in per-loop mean occupancy, so a length distribution matters even when the total DNA and total DSB count are held fixed.
next_steps: Download a public Hi-C loop-domain call set (e.g., HFFc6 or GM12878 from 4DN). Compute the empirical loop-length CDF. Replace the single-N_L Poisson kernel in globle_static.py with a size-weighted mixture over loop lengths. Re-run the RT112 dose-response and compare against the uniform-loop baseline. Also perform a one-at-a-time sensitivity sweep on N_L, mean-loop-length, and shape parameter.

q: How does GLDM-style DSB-cluster prediction interact with modern DSB-repair pathway modeling (NHEJ vs HR vs alt-EJ balance, cell-cycle phase, repair-kinetics competition)?
basis: GLDM in its 2012 static form treats a clustered lesion as irreversibly lethal with weight eps_c, folding all downstream biology into two fitted per-cell constants. Repair-pathway choice (NHEJ vs HR) is cell-cycle dependent and lesion-complexity dependent, and modern repair-kinetics models (e.g., MEDRAS, DSBrepair, TRAX-CHEM) resolve this explicitly.
next_steps: Couple the GLDM cluster-probability output p_c(D) to a two-compartment ODE repair model with distinct rate constants for isolated vs clustered breaks, and compare against the fully-empirical eps_i / eps_c fits. Use published RT112 or HSG time-course gamma-H2AX foci data as a target. Test whether a mechanistic (repair-rate + misrepair-probability) parameterisation predicts (eps_i, eps_c) rather than absorbing them as free constants.

q: Does GLDM correctly predict the isoeffective dose reduction observed under FLASH ultra-high-dose-rate radiotherapy, or does the dose-rate-independent static formulation miss FLASH sparing entirely?
basis: Static GLDM has no time axis: it is a per-fraction dose-response with no repair kinetics or radical chemistry. FLASH radiotherapy (>= 40 Gy/s) shows normal-tissue sparing that is dose-rate dependent, hypothesized to involve transient oxygen depletion or radical recombination on sub-second timescales. A model with no time axis cannot mechanistically predict FLASH sparing, but the question is whether the eps_c cluster-lethality weight is empirically dose-rate-invariant.
next_steps: Pull published FLASH vs conventional survival curves for a matched cell line (e.g., zebrafish embryo, mouse intestinal crypt, or clonogenic in vitro). Fit static GLDM under conventional dose rate to extract (eps_i, eps_c); then attempt to fit the FLASH curve. If GLDM cannot fit both with a single parameter set, quantify the residual and propose a minimal FLASH extension (e.g., dose-rate-dependent effective eps_c). The kinetic-GLOBLE branch (Herr 2014) is the natural bridge.

q: Can an ML-based cluster-severity scoring function, trained on nanoscale track-structure Monte Carlo (PARTRAC / TOPAS-nBio) DSB spectra, replace the binary isolated-vs-clustered distinction and improve predictive accuracy across radiation qualities?
basis: GLDM's binary classification collapses cluster complexity into a single indicator (1 vs >=2 DSBs per loop). Track-structure MC produces a full spectrum of cluster complexity (number of breaks, spatial spread, associated base damages) that is known to correlate with residual damage and misrepair probability. An ML scorer trained on MC-derived cluster fingerprints could give a continuous severity weight.
next_steps: Use a public TOPAS-nBio or Geant4-DNA output (or generate a small one on a free endpoint) to build a training set of (cluster-fingerprint, empirical lethality-weight) pairs. Train a lightweight gradient-boosted regressor or shallow MLP to predict per-cluster lethality. Plug the resulting severity function into the GLDM survival integral, replacing the binary eps_i / eps_c. Compare against the 17-line clonogenic panel used here for baseline, and extend to a proton or carbon-ion dataset to test the radiation-quality generalisation the paper's downstream ion-GLOBLE work targets.
